title: Importance of designing scalable, reliable, and maintainable systems
summary: Why scalability, reliability, and maintainability are the three constraints that drive every high-level design decision, and how to trade them off explicitly.

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: High-level design is not drawing boxes. It is deciding **how the system behaves when load grows 10x, when parts fail daily, and when three teams change it at once.** If your design cannot answer those three pressures, it is a diagram, not a design. Every load balancer, replica, queue, and module boundary exists to buy room against one of those pressures — and every one charges you complexity in return.
What the three words actually mean

Interviewers use these words loosely. You should use them precisely. **Scalability** is the ability to sustain higher load with acceptable latency by adding resources, without a rewrite. Load means requests per second, concurrent connections, data size, and fan-out work per request. Acceptable means you name a latency bound — usually p95 or p99, not average — at that load. **Reliability** is the probability the system does what its contract says over a time window, despite faults. That includes returning correct data, not just returning *something*. A fast wrong answer is a reliability failure. **Maintainability** is how cheaply a team other than the original authors can understand, change, and operate the system without causing an outage. It is measured in time to add a feature, time to diagnose an incident, and blast radius of a bad deploy. The trade-off that ties them together: each property is purchased with indirection — load balancers, replicas, caches, queues, interfaces — and every layer of indirection makes the system harder to reason about.

These three are HLD concerns because they dictate shape, not code. You can fix a slow function with better code. You cannot fix a stateful single server, a single-region primary with no replica, or a monolith where every team edits the same deploy unit by tuning code. Those choices lock in your ceiling for growth, your failure modes, and your velocity. That is why interviewers start here: if you get the shape wrong, no low-level cleverness saves you. State the target numbers first — expected reads and writes per second, data growth per year, availability target, team size — then let those numbers force the boxes.
The mechanism: where load, failure, and change hit

Think of a request path as three gauntlets. First, **load concentration**: too many requests arrive at one choke point — a single server, a single database primary, a hot partition. The fix is always some form of spreading: replicate compute, partition data, or shed and defer work. Second, **fault propagation**: any component will fail — process crash, disk loss, zone outage, slow dependency. Without isolation the fault cascades and takes the whole path down with it. The fix is redundancy plus boundaries: health checks, timeouts, retries with backoff, bulkheads, and failover. Third, **change coupling**: every deploy, schema change, or config edit risks every caller. Without seams the system freezes because nobody dares touch it. The fix is modular ownership: explicit APIs, versioned contracts, backward-compatible storage, and independent deploy units. Good HLD puts a specific mechanism at each gauntlet and can say why that mechanism and not the alternative.

blocks.text: Read the diagram as decisions, not decoration. The load balancer exists so compute can scale horizontally: add stateless app instances and no session state has to move. That choice is why the app tier must be stateless — stickiness would reintroduce concentration and make autoscaling unsafe. The cache exists to absorb read skew so the database does not have to scale linearly with reads, but it introduces a second source of truth and an invalidation problem you now own. The queue exists to absorb write bursts and decouple slow work from user-facing latency, but it turns a synchronous error into a delayed one and forces you to design for at-least-once delivery. The replica exists so a single node loss does not lose data or stop reads, but it forces a consistency choice: synchronous replication protects data and taxes write latency, asynchronous replication protects latency and risks loss on failover. Every arrow that helps one property hurts another. Name it out loud.
Scalability, quantified

Scalability has two primitives. **Vertical scaling** — bigger machine — is simple, needs no partitioning logic, preserves strong consistency easily, and fails hard at a ceiling. You hit physical limits, cost goes superlinear, and you still have a single failure domain. Use it to delay complexity, not to avoid it. **Horizontal scaling** — more machines — has no hard ceiling but demands that work be splittable. That requires three preconditions most candidates skip: stateless request handling or externalised session state so any node can serve any request, a partition strategy so data and hot keys spread evenly, and a load distribution layer that actually observes health and load rather than blindly round-robining. Without those, adding nodes adds contention, not capacity. The classic proof is a relational primary taking all writes: you can add fifty app servers and write throughput does not move because the primary is the serial bottleneck. The trade-off: horizontal scale buys near-linear growth and fault isolation at the price of distributed-systems problems — routing, rebalancing, skewed partitions, and cross-partition operations that suddenly need two-phase logic or denormalisation.

blocks.text: Reliability is math plus paranoia

Reliability is not vibes; it is arithmetic over failure and repair. Availability is uptime divided by total time, often expressed in nines: 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month, 99.99% allows about 4 minutes. Two levers move it: how often things break and how fast you recover. Most mature systems win on the second lever because hardware, networks, and deploys *will* break weekly. That is why HLD favours fast detection and fast failover — health checks in seconds, automated promotion of a replica, traffic shift away from a bad zone — over heroic prevention. Redundancy without fast repair is decoration: a standby replica you cannot promote in minutes is just cost. And redundancy without isolation is shared fate: two copies in the same rack, same config push, or same synchronous dependency fail together. The trade-off: every nine you add roughly doubles the operational machinery — multi-zone or multi-region deployment, quorum writes, chaos testing, runbooks, on-call load — while user-perceived benefit shrinks. Do not promise four nines for a v1 feed; promise it where downtime costs money or trust, and show where you deliberately accept lower guarantees.

items: **Timeouts on everything.** No unbounded waits. A missing timeout turns one slow dependency into thread exhaustion across the whole tier. Set aggressive timeouts and enforce them at the client, not just the server.
**Retries with exponential backoff and jitter, only for idempotent work.** Blind retry amplifies an outage into a retry storm. Require an idempotency key for writes and cap attempts.
**Bulkheads and circuit breakers.** Isolate thread pools, connection pools, and quotas per dependency so one bad downstream cannot drown the others. Open the circuit fast and fail visibly.

**Replication with a tested failover path.** A primary plus an untested replica is a single point of failure with extra steps. Automate promotion, practice it, and decide upfront: lose writes or lose availability on partition.

**Durability before acknowledgement.** Acknowledge a write only after it is on multiple durable nodes or a durable log. Anything else trades acknowledged data for latency — sometimes correct, never accidental.

blocks.text: Maintainability decides whether v2 ever ships

Systems die more often from unchangeability than from load. Maintainability at HLD means three things: you can find the problem, you can change one part without breaking the rest, and you can roll out safely. That translates to small deploy units with clear owners, explicit versioned APIs between them, storage schemas that evolve backward-compatibly, and observability built in — structured logs with request IDs, metrics on latency and saturation, traces across service hops. Monoliths win early here: one repo, one deploy, atomic refactors. They lose when team count grows and every change contends on the same release train. Services win on team autonomy and independent scaling but charge a permanent tax: network failures, version skew, distributed debugging, and contract governance. The trade-off to voice: modularity slows the first launch and speeds the tenth. Choose seams along failure and ownership boundaries — auth, billing, feed ranking — not along entities that change together.

items: Explicit API contracts with versioning, so callers do not break on deploy.
Backward-compatible data evolution: add nullable fields, dual-write then migrate, never rename in place.
Independent deployability with fast rollback — small blast radius beats big-bang releases.
End-to-end observability: one request ID from edge to database, dashboards for the four golden signals.
Runbooks and ownership: every box on the diagram has an owner and a known recovery step.

blocks.text: How it fails in production, and the symptom you would see

When these properties are missing, production tells you in specific ways. An unscalable design does not fail politely at peak; latency climbs non-linearly, queues deepen, then timeouts cascade and the system sheds load by collapsing. An unreliable design does not just go down; it corrupts or loses acknowledged work, serves stale data as if fresh, or flaps between zones because failover was never rehearsed. An unmaintainable design does not explode; it calcifies — deploys move to Friday-night windows, a one-line change needs five team approvals, and incidents take hours because no trace connects the edge to the failing store. Learn to map symptom to missing mechanism: that mapping is what interviewers probe with follow-ups.

items: **p99 spikes while average looks fine → hot partition or cache miss storm.** Symptom: a few keys dominate one shard or one cache expiry triggers a flood to the database. Fix is key splitting, jittered TTLs, and request coalescing — not more identical nodes.

**Retry storm after a partial outage → no backoff, no idempotency.** Symptom: downstream recovers, then immediately drowns again under duplicated retries. Cap retries, add jitter, gate with circuit breakers.

**Acknowledged writes vanish after failover → async replication assumed durable.** Symptom: users re-create content that was confirmed. Either make replication synchronous on the critical path or acknowledge only after quorum.

**Deploy takes down unrelated features → shared fate, no bulkhead.** Symptom: a config push or schema migration halts everything. Split deploy units, feature-flag risky changes, keep backward compatibility.

**Incident takes hours to locate → no correlation IDs or saturation metrics.** Symptom: five dashboards disagree and nobody knows which hop is slow. Propagate request IDs, trace cross-service calls, alert on queue depth and pool saturation, not just CPU.

blocks.text: How this shows up in an HLD interview

items.title: You are asked to state non-functionals first
items.text: Do not jump to boxes. Convert vague goals into numbers: requests per second, read-write ratio, payload size, retention, p95 target, availability target. This tells the interviewer which property dominates. A read-heavy feed pushes cache and replicas; a payment ledger pushes durability and correctness over raw scale.

items.title: You are asked to pick stateless vs stateful and why
items.text: Say it directly: app servers stay stateless so they scale and drain safely; state lives in stores built for it. If you propose sticky sessions, justify what breaks when an instance dies and how deploy works without dropping connections.

items.title: You are asked to handle a spike and a failure
items.text: Expect two follow-ups: what happens at 10x traffic, and what happens when the database or a zone dies. Answer with mechanisms: autoscale policy plus queue depth for the spike, replica promotion plus traffic shift for the failure. Name what degrades first and what the user sees.

items.title: You are asked to evolve the design
items.text: Add a feature, change the schema, split a service. Show seams: versioned APIs, dual-write migration, feature flags, independent deploys. This is the maintainability check most candidates fail because they drew hard-wired boxes.

items.title: You are asked to justify what you did not build
items.text: Strong answers end with deliberate no's: no multi-region active-active yet because operational cost outweighs the availability gain at this scale; no microservices sprawl because two teams do not need eight deploy units. Interviewers promote candidates who price their choices.

blocks.title: What the interviewer is scoring
blocks.text: They are not counting boxes. They are listening for: did you quantify load, did you isolate faults with a concrete recovery path, and did you leave seams for change? Every proposal should end with its cost. If you cannot say what you sacrificed, you did not design — you drew.
Misconceptions that get you downleveled

items: **Scalable means fast.** No. Scalable means throughput grows with resources while latency stays bounded. A single-threaded in-memory sort can be fast and entirely unscalable beyond one box.
**More servers always means more capacity.** Only if the bottleneck is parallelisable. A single primary, a hot shard, or a shared lock makes extra nodes idle while the choke point burns.

**Reliable means never failing.** Real reliability assumes constant failure and optimises recovery: detection in seconds, failover in minutes, no data loss on the acknowledged path. Prevention alone is fantasy.

**Async and eventual consistency are free performance.** They move cost, not remove it: reconciliation jobs, user-visible delay, duplicate handling, and harder debugging. Use them where staleness is tolerable, not by default.

**Maintainable means more services.** Splitting a ball of mud into distributed mud increases ownership cost without reducing coupling. Maintainability comes from stable contracts and independent deploys, whether inside one repo or five.

blocks.text: The senior move is to make the deferral safe. Build a modular monolith with clear interfaces so extraction later does not require a rewrite. Keep the app tier stateless from day one because retrofitting statelessness is painful. Put writes behind an append-only log or primary with replicas even if you run one copy initially, so promotion is a config change rather than a redesign. In the interview, phrase it as staging: what you ship in month one, what breaks first at 10x, and what pre-planned seam lets you scale, harden, or split without throwing the system away. That narrative proves you understand cost, not just catalog parts.

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: Say: **I design for load with stateless horizontal scale and partitioning, for faults with redundancy plus fast, tested recovery, and for change with versioned contracts and independent deploys — and I only pay for each where the numbers justify it.** Then point to the numbers.
